q: Which of these lines are compile errors? Select all that apply.
explain: `a` matches the shape exactly. `b` fails because `"huge"` isn't one of the three strings in `Size`; a literal union only allows the listed values. `c` fails because `size` is missing, and every property in an object type is required unless marked optional. `d` fails because `extraCheese` isn't part of `Pizza`: an object literal written straight into a typed variable may only have known properties, which is how TypeScript catches misspelled property names.

q: Why does the last line fail to compile?
options: `let next = "placed"` is inferred as `string`, and a `string` could be any text, not just a `Status`
Literal unions only work with `const` functions
explain: With `let`, TypeScript assumes you might reassign the variable to any other string, so it widens the type to `string`. A `string` isn't assignable to `"placed" | "delivered"`. Fix it with `const next = "placed"` (inferred as the literal `"placed"`) or with `let next: Status = "placed"`. The spelling is fine, and capital `String` is the wrapper object type, which would make things worse, not better.

`same = first` doesn't copy the object. Both names point at the **same** object, so changing it through `same` changes what `first` sees too. `const` only stops you from pointing `first` at a different object; it doesn't freeze the properties. That's why functions that "update" an order should return a **new** object instead of assigning to the one they were given.

q: You `console.log(order)` and see `{ id: 7, status: 'cooking' }`. Where did the `Order` type go?
options: It was erased. Types are only checked while you write code; the JavaScript that runs contains values, not types
Type aliases are stored on the object as a hidden property
It only shows up in the browser console, not in Node
explain: A `type` alias produces no code at all. After compiling, the program is plain JavaScript with no trace of `Order`. `typeof order` at runtime prints `"object"`, the JavaScript category of the value. TypeScript's job ends before the program starts: it has already checked that every place using `order` matches the shape.
